job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a backend developer at a small start-up in Vancouver that builds scheduling software for physiotherapy clinics. Most mornings I open my laptop in a shared flat above a bubble tea shop, ask an AI assistant to sketch a function, then fix what it gets wrong. In the afternoon I'm in a call with our founder, Dana, and two other developers. In the evenings I work on a side project, a free app that helps tenants in my building track repair requests. I like the speed, and I'm tired because everything moves so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, my tools are already useful and that's enough. I'd tell friends hype is annoying, but small gains add up. At work I'd just keep shipping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be happy. If AI only trims routine tasks, I get the benefits without the chaos. My worry in that world is the same as today: rent in Vancouver and a start-up that might run out of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep the day job, keep building the tenant app at night and try to get a few buildings using it. I'd also keep six months of savings and maybe invest a bit in an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with the normal start-up jitters about funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the start-up might run out of money. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana told us we have about fourteen months of runway. If a big clinic chain signs, we're fine, and if not, we'd all be looking. I'd find another job in weeks, I think, because my references are strong, but it would still sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the tenant app. What's the plan for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's free, open source, and three buildings in my neighbourhood use it. My idea is a tenants' union could use it to show a landlord the record of ignored repairs. I'm not trying to make money, which is probably why it's fun.

say: My tools are useful already, and **small gains add up**.
I'd keep shipping at work and tell friends the hype is tiring.
think: I get the **benefits without the chaos**, so I'm happy.
My real worry is **rent** and a start-up with fourteen months of runway.
do: Keep the day job and build the **tenant app** at night.
Hold **six months** of savings and put a bit into an index fund.
feel: I feel **calm**, with normal start-up jitters about money.
S0.quote: I'm not trying to make money, which is probably why it's fun.
fieldNote: He is secure because **employers want him**, but the start-up's runway adds a background worry.
The tenant app shows his progressive streak in practice.
He uses AI daily and sees it as a tool, not a threat.

steps.text: Get five more buildings using the free tenant repair app
Put 300 a month into an index fund
Keep six months of rent in a plain savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the job changes, and I'm in the right place. I'd tell friends that writing code is turning into reviewing code. At work I'd propose we build the product around AI agents, not just use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the entry-level coding jobs are the ones going. A lot of firms won't hire juniors if an assistant does the junior's work. I'm lucky that I'm already in, but I'd worry about a friend from uni who's still applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to manage AI agents properly, how to test them, how to spot their mistakes. I'd move from writing functions to designing systems, which means studying architecture in the evenings. And I'd push our tenant app harder, because it's a way to have something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at the same time. It's like surfing, you're moving fast and you can still fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a friend still applying. What's going on there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq did the same degree and sent 80 applications with five interviews and no offers. He's living with his parents. I told him to contribute to an open source project, and I gave him a reference, but I can't make a hiring manager see him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does that leave your own seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's safe for now because I can use the tools and the firm is small. But if Dana can run the company with three developers instead of four, I'm not sure I'd be one of the three. So I want to be the person who understands the whole system.

say: Writing code is turning into **reviewing code**, and I'm in the right place.
I'd propose we build the product around AI agents.
think: **Entry-level** coding jobs are going, as firms skip juniors when an assistant does the work.
My seat is safe now, but a smaller team could cut me.
do: Learn to test and manage **AI agents** and study system architecture in the evenings.
Push the **tenant app** harder as something of my own.
feel: I feel **excited and uneasy**, like surfing fast with a chance to fall.
S1.quote: Writing code is turning into reviewing code.
fieldNote: He sees the shift as an **opening**, but has a friend as a warning.
He knows his seat depends on a small company's size.
He wants a role at the **system level**, not at the function level.

steps.text: Study software architecture two evenings a week
Learn to test and supervise AI coding agents at work
Help my friend Tariq with a portfolio and give a reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and not many people are ready. Online I'd write that we need a basic income trial and public AI tools, not only private ones. At work I'd ask Dana what the company's role would be in a world where anyone can build our product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of software jobs vanish in two years, mine included. Our product is the sort a good AI can rebuild in a weekend. I'd be angry at a system that makes a few investors richer while everyone else scrambles, but I'm also curious about what I could build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put aside nearly all my paycheque, cut spending to the bone and aim to have a year of rent saved. I'd go full-time on the tenant app and try to turn it into a worker-owned or tenant-owned co-op. And I'd join a political campaign for public ownership of AI tools, because I think this isn't something to leave to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and wired. I'd barely sleep, and I'd also feel strangely awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go full-time on the tenant app. What would that mean for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have my savings and a lower living cost if I shared a room again. Maybe 18 months before it runs dry. I'd also ask my parents in Burnaby for dinner and a plan, because they've been through harder things. My dad ran a restaurant that closed twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a tenant-owned co-op actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would own the software, charge buildings a small fee and share the profits among members. It's not a fantasy, because tenant unions already exist, and an AI would help us run it with almost no staff. If AI makes work cheap, I want ownership to be spread out.

say: I'd ask for a **basic income trial** and public AI tools.
At work I'd ask what a company like ours is for when anyone can build the product.
think: A lot of software jobs vanish in two years, **including mine**.
I'm angry at a system that enriches a few investors and curious about what I could build.
do: Save nearly all my pay and aim for a year of **rent** in the bank.
Go full-time on the tenant app and try a **tenant-owned co-op**.
feel: I feel **scared and wired**, barely sleeping yet strangely awake.
S2.quote: If AI makes work cheap, I want ownership to be spread out.
fieldNote: His reaction is to **build something shared**, not just protect himself.
He expects his own job to go but stays energised.
Savings and family give him 18 months of runway, which keeps him anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Save nearly all my pay until I have a year of rent
Work full-time on the tenant app and try a tenant-owned co-op
Join a campaign for public ownership of AI tools
Ask my parents in Burnaby for dinner and a plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something real. I'd tell people to start small projects now. At work I'd say let's find the parts of our product that depend on people and trust, not just code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2031 a lot of what I do is automated. I'd still be employable, because I'd be the person who knows how the machines run. I'd want to be in a company I partly own, though, so the gains aren't all up the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend two years on the tenant app and my own tools, and one year moving into a role that looks after AI systems. I'd learn some law and policy, because the rules are going to matter. I'd also buy a small share in a start-up through a friend's angel group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with some worry. I feel I have a plan, and that's what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn some law and policy. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the rules about who's liable when an AI makes a mistake will shape everything. I read a bit about the EU's AI rules last year, and what struck me is nobody agrees on who is responsible. A developer who understands both could be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about friends who aren't as quick with this stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that bothers me. Tariq and my cousin Mei are bright but slower with new tools, and I can't carry everyone. I'd try to run a small study group on weekends, because teaching is the best way to learn it.

say: Five years is enough to build something **real**, so start small projects now.
I'd tell my team to find the parts of our product that rely on trust.
think: By 2031 much of my work is automated, but I'd be the one who knows **how the machines run**.
I want a company I partly own, so gains aren't all up the chain.
do: Spend two years on the tenant app and then move into **AI systems oversight**.
Learn some **law and policy** and join a friend's angel group.
feel: I feel **hopeful with some worry**, because I have a plan.
S3.quote: Teaching is the best way to learn it.
fieldNote: Time gives him a **plan**, and he leans on skills, ownership and law.
He worries about slower friends and wants to help them.
He stays uneasy since his firm's survival is uncertain.

steps.text: Read the AI liability rules and take an evening law course
Join a friend's angel group and buy a small stake in a start-up
Run a weekend study group for friends who are slower with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty. I'd say this is the best time in history to learn. At work I'd just keep experimenting and share what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm optimistic, and I know that's partly luck. I'm young, I've got a good degree and my family can back me. I'd worry about people who don't have those cushions, and I'd say so online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep building, maybe start a small company with Tariq and a couple of others around year three. I'd buy a place with a few friends, as a co-op housing share. I'd save and vote for the policies I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. It's a bit like a long summer, with some storms in the distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know your optimism is partly luck. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'd been born into a family with debts or a smaller city, I'd have the same brain and a much harder time. My parents paid for my first-year rent and I never had to work in a cafe during exams. I'd like to spend part of my twenties making that less of a lottery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give time to a free coding class at the library, and I'd put 5 percent of my pay into a tenants' fund. It isn't much, but it's what I can start with. I'd also push for public money for training, because charity alone won't cover it.

say: Ten years is plenty, and it's the **best time** in history to learn.
I'd share what works from my experiments at work.
think: I'm optimistic, and partly that's **luck**: a good degree and family backing.
I worry about people without those cushions and I'd say so.
do: Start a small company with **Tariq** and others around year three.
Buy a place in a **co-op housing** share with friends.
feel: I feel **pretty good**, like a long summer with storms far away.
S4.quote: My parents paid for my first-year rent and I never had to work in a cafe during exams.
fieldNote: He **names his own luck** and wants to spread it.
Ten years makes him comfortable, and his worry is for others.
His plans combine business, housing and charity.

steps.text: Start a small software company with Tariq in year three
Buy a co-op housing share with friends
Teach a free coding class at the local library each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it's too fast for anyone to build fair rules. What would help is a basic income trial, public AI tools anyone can use and tenant and worker ownership models that actually get funding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume the fast adopters are all selfish. A lot of us use the tools every day and still care about the person next to us, and want rules that protect them.

headlineQuote: If I'd been born into a family with debts or a smaller city, I'd have the same brain and a much harder time.
portrait: Umar is a **22-year-old** backend developer at a Vancouver start-up, top of his class with two internships.
He uses AI tools **every day** and builds a free app for tenants at night.
He is progressive, aware that family backing is **luck**, and wants ownership spread out.
He is calm when little changes and **anxious** only when two years leave no time for fair rules.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because it is too fast to build fair rules.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income trial**, public AI tools and funding for tenant and worker ownership.
